name: Gleam
title: Gleam (1.19)

type.text: **Static types with full inference**: A function's types are checked at compile time, and an annotation is optional almost everywhere
**A custom type is the only way to add a case**: A `case` over a custom type is checked for exhaustiveness, so a new variant breaks every site that must handle it
**There is no null**: Absence is `Option(a)`, and the compiler rejects a use of the option as a plain value
**There is no inheritance and no class**: Data is a custom type and behaviour is a function, so there is no hierarchy to couple to
**An opaque type hides its representation**: A module can export a type without its constructor, so the invariant is enforced at the module boundary
**Generics are parametric and checked**: `Result(a, e)`, `List(a)`, and a user type take type parameters with no cast
**There are no type classes or traits**: Reuse across types goes through a record of functions passed to a generic function, not through a shared interface
**A call's effects are not in its type**: A signature says what a function returns, not that it reads a process dictionary, sends a message, or panics
**The foreign boundary is a promise**: An external function names its Erlang or JavaScript counterpart by hand, and nothing checks that the two agree

construction.text: **A constructor is the only way to make a value**: A custom type's constructor checks every field, and a case cannot build one that the type does not declare
**A record updates by copy**: `Person(..person, name: "Ada")` returns a new value and leaves the original alone
**A module holds functions, not mutable state**: There is no global variable to read or write during construction
**Construction is explicit**: There are no default values and no implicit conversions, so every field is passed at the call site

memory.text: **The BEAM collects each process separately**: A process has its own heap, and the pause is the runtime's to schedule
**Data is immutable**: A value is never changed in place, so two holders cannot disagree about its contents
**A process owns its heap**: A value is copied between processes, so no reference is shared across a process boundary
**There is no manual deallocation**: The runtime frees memory, so a double free or a use after free cannot occur
**No destructor runs at scope exit**: A resource follows the process lifetime or an explicit close, not a block boundary

error.text: **A failure is a value**: A fallible function returns `Result(a, e)`, and the type says so
**`use` threads the failure path**: `use x <- result.try(f())` returns a failure to the caller without a match at each step
**A panic is a process crash**: `panic` ends the process and is not a channel for a recoverable failure
**The error type is the module's choice**: Nothing in the language forces one error type across modules

concurrency.text: **A process is the unit of concurrency**: A Gleam process is an Erlang process with its own heap and mailbox
**A message replaces shared memory**: Two processes exchange a value by copy, so a data race between them cannot occur
**OTP supervises the tree**: A supervisor restarts a failed child, so failure handling is a supervision tree rather than a `try` block
**There is no second function kind**: A function does not become `async`; the runtime schedules processes, so no colour spreads through the call graph
**The actor library is a package**: `gleam_otp` supplies the actor and supervisor abstractions, so their version is a dependency

platform.text: **One source compiles to two runtimes**: `gleam build --target erlang` emits for the BEAM and `--target javascript` emits for Node and the browser
**The Erlang back end emits abstract forms**: The compiler produces Erlang's intermediate representation and skips the Erlang front end, so a crash report names a Gleam line
**Interop on the BEAM is zero-cost**: A Gleam module and an Erlang or Elixir module call each other without a marshalling layer
**The two targets have different runtimes**: A program that runs on both meets the BEAM scheduler on one target and the JavaScript event loop on the other

performance.text: **The compiler is fast**: A full build of the published benchmark project completes in a fraction of a second, and a rebuild is incremental
**A collection pause is part of the timing**: The BEAM collects a process independently, and the pause is a latency budget's cost
**The BEAM compiles the hot path**: The runtime's JIT compiles a hot function, so a long-running service does not run interpreted
**The JavaScript target inherits the engine's limits**: Speed on that target is the JavaScript engine's, not the language's

ecosystem.text: **`gleam add` and Hex are the whole dependency story**: A manifest, a lockfile, and a central registry are part of the toolchain
**One binary holds the toolchain**: `build`, `format`, `test`, `add`, and the language server ship together
**The ecosystem is small**: The package pool is younger and thinner than the mainstream registries, so more code is written than found
**The BEAM ecosystem is reachable**: A project can depend on Erlang and Elixir packages and call them directly
**The language is young**: A library can change quickly, and a tutorial can lag a release
The NIF ABI is versioned and checked at load on the BEAM runtime it runs on [@erlNif]

evolution.text: **Releases follow semantic versioning**: A 1.x release keeps the language compatible, and a package states the version it requires
**The cadence is short**: A release arrives every six to eight weeks, so a fix is not held for a year
**Mechanical migrations ship with the compiler**: A deprecation arrives with a fix in the compiler or the formatter
**A pre-1.0 package can break**: A dependency that has not reached 1.0 may change in a breaking release

domain.text: **A web service is the ordinary project**: Wisp and the OTP libraries make an HTTP service the default shape
**The browser is a supported target**: Lustre compiles a Gleam program to the front end through the JavaScript target
**A command-line tool is supported**: An escript packages a single-file program for the BEAM
**The centre is server-side**: Examples, packages, and hiring lean toward backend work on the BEAM

learning.text: **The language is small**: The official tour covers the whole language in an afternoon
**An error carries the fix**: The compiler names the mismatch and often prints the corrected code
**The language server is the compiler**: Completion, rename, and go-to-definition come from the same binary
**Inference hides a type at the boundary**: A reader sometimes has to ask the editor for an inferred type

syntax.text: **Every construct is an expression**: A `case`, a `let`, and a function body produce a value, so a value is defined where it is computed
**The pipeline reads left to right**: `value |> f |> g` states the data flow without an intermediate name
**A label names the argument at the call site**: `request.new(method: Get, path: "/")` reads without the definition
**The braces and commas are load-bearing**: The syntax is small but strict, and a missing comma is a compile error

testing.text: **`gleam test` runs the suite**: The toolchain discovers and runs the test modules
**`gleeunit` is the standard harness**: A test is a function, and a failed assertion stops the module
**The compiler checks the test**: A test is type-checked with the project, so a broken test does not compile
**The harness is a package**: `gleeunit` is a dependency, and its version must match the compiler's expectations

security.text: **Memory safety belongs to the runtime**: A program cannot read or write outside its data, and the language has no `unsafe`
**Immutability removes a class of bugs**: A value cannot change under a holder
**There is no `eval`**: The language has no construct that turns a string into code
**The foreign boundary is unchecked**: An external function's signature is a promise, and the other runtime does not verify it

reproducibility.text: **The build does not check reproducibility**: `gleam build` writes BEAM or JavaScript output and never compares a rebuild against a published artifact, so a consumer cannot confirm the two match

supplychain.text: **A package carries no build attestation**: The registry signs its own index, but nothing in a release states who built it or from what source, so a compromised build is not distinguishable from a genuine one
**Hex names are global**: A package name is unique across the registry, so an owner is not separated by a namespace

observability.text: **No tracing standard is part of the language**: A project chooses an OpenTelemetry package and its own conventions, and the standard library states none

feedback.text: **The compiler is the language server**: An error is reported in the editor as the file is saved, and a rebuild is incremental

interop.text: **Interop is a language feature**: A module calls Erlang, Elixir, or JavaScript through a declared external function, so the boundary is written down

tradeoffs: **A small ecosystem is the price of a young language**: Fewer packages mean more code written locally; this is a community outcome, not a language mechanism
**Two targets, two runtimes**: A program that runs on the BEAM and in JavaScript meets two schedulers and two sets of libraries
**No OOP is a deliberate subtraction**: Reuse goes through functions and records, so a team accustomed to inheritance rewrites its habits
**The foreign boundary is untyped**: An external function is a hand-written promise on both the Erlang and the JavaScript side
**Immutability copies at the process boundary**: A message is copied between processes, which is safe and not free
**The cadence is fast and the language is young**: A short release cycle is a fix rate and a moving target
verdict: Gleam's design yields low language-imposed coupling. Static inference removes the dynamic-typing mechanisms, custom types and exhaustive matching remove the missing-sum-type mechanism, and `Option` and `Result` put absence and failure in the type. The BEAM gives it process isolation, so no shared-memory race is expressible, and it avoids function colouring because a process, not an `async` function, is the unit of concurrency. Main strength: a small language whose defaults — immutability, exhaustive matching, errors as values — leave few coupling mechanisms to price. Main weakness: the ecosystem is young and thin, the foreign boundary is unchecked, and the runtime's collector still schedules the heap.

energy.text: Runs on the BEAM, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it less reliably than a mainstream language [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: A hex package ships source compiled to BEAM bytecode
The NIF API version compiles into the library, and the runtime checks it at load
